analysis.one_liner: Mandates federal safety tests so dressers and chests cannot tip over on children.
analysis.headline: The House passed the STURDY Act by voice vote with no recorded opposition in September 2019, but the Senate Commerce Committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Dressers and chests of drawers that tip over kill and injure young children each year, often when kids climb on open drawers. The STURDY Act would require the Consumer Product Safety Commission to replace the existing voluntary furniture stability standard with a mandatory one: tests simulating a child up to 60 pounds pulling on drawers, tests under real-world conditions like carpeting and loaded or multiple open drawers, coverage of shorter units, and stronger warning labels. It passed the House without opposition but never got a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children, who would get dressers and chests tested to survive real-world tip-over scenarios, and the safety advocates who have pushed for a mandatory standard after decades of tip-over deaths.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CPSC, within one year, to issue a mandatory consumer product safety standard for clothing storage units to protect children from tip-over-related death or injury, replacing reliance on the voluntary standard.

The standard must include tests simulating children up to 60 pounds, objective and repeatable tests simulating real-world use including carpeted surfaces, loaded drawers, multiple open drawers, and dynamic force, and testing of all units including those under 30 inches tall.
The standard must include warning requirements based on ASTM F2057-17, and directs the CPSC to strengthen those requirements if reasonably necessary to protect children.

analysis.who_pays: Furniture manufacturers and importers, who would bear testing, redesign, and compliance costs to meet the new mandatory standard, with some of that cost likely passed to shoppers as slightly higher furniture prices.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers, including craft and handmade furniture makers the bill consults, would bear new testing and redesign costs to meet the mandatory standard, which could raise prices for consumers.

The bill gives the CPSC only one year to assess the voluntary standards and issue a final rule, a timeline some would consider tight for a formal rulemaking, though it does allow the agency to update the standard later as needed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is concrete: a mandatory, realistic tip-over test for a product that kills and injures young children. The costs are ordinary regulatory compliance costs for the furniture industry, likely modest in the price of a dresser, and the bill preserves the agency's ability to fine-tune the standard later. The design is straightforward and the trade-off favors the safety requirement.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote with no opposition, but the Senate Commerce Committee sat on it for the remaining sixteen months of the Congress, and it expired without a Senate vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the STURDY Act on April 10, 2019, and it drew 23 cosponsors, all House Democrats.
The House Energy and Commerce Committee marked the bill up and reported it as amended by voice vote on September 16, 2019.
The House passed the bill on September 17, 2019 under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure used for noncontroversial bills, agreeing by voice vote with no recorded opposition.

The Senate received the bill on September 18, 2019 and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Furniture manufacturers came out ahead: they kept selling under the existing voluntary standard, with no mandatory tip-over testing, warning upgrades, or redesign costs. Families with young children did not get the stronger protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Furniture makers, avoiding mandatory safety tests

for.name: Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and moved to suspend the rules and pass it on the House floor.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Held subcommittee hearings and markups, ordered the bill reported as amended by voice vote, and reported it to the House with H. Rept. 116-209.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the House-passed bill on September 18, 2019 and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, markup, or floor referral — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Roger Wicker
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee action or sent it to the Senate floor after the House passed it without opposition.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic cosponsors, but the House passed it by voice vote with no member asking for a recorded vote or speaking against it, signaling no meaningful opposition in the chamber.

industries.note: The bill would replace the voluntary ASTM F2057 stability standard with a mandatory federal rule covering all clothing storage units, including units under 30 inches, requiring realistic tip-over testing and stronger warnings. That imposes testing and redesign costs on the industry, and the cost of avoiding those requirements was that the bill died in the Senate.
